content.title: About
content.content: Red pepper, cooked, is the mature fruit of sweet pepper (Capsicum annuum) that has been boiled until tender. Cooking retains many nutrients while giving the pepper a milder, slightly sweet flavor.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Cooked red pepper contains a higher level of vitamin C than its green or yellow counterparts.
Heat destroys part of capsaicin, making the taste less spicy.
It is widely used in Mediterranean and Asian cuisines in soups, stews, and sauces.
Cooking can enhance aromatic compounds, improving overall flavor perception.

items.title: Rich in vitamin C
items.content: A 100 g serving provides over 150 % of the daily value of vitamin C, supporting immune function and antioxidant protection.

items.title: Source of vitamin A
items.content: Beta‑carotene, which converts to vitamin A, promotes healthy vision and skin.

items.title: Contains vitamin B6
items.content: Vitamin B6 is involved in protein metabolism and neurotransmitter synthesis.

items.title: Provides dietary fiber
items.content: Fiber aids digestion and contributes to a feeling of fullness.

items.title: Minerals: potassium and iron
items.content: Potassium helps maintain fluid balance, while iron is essential for blood formation.

items.title: Pepper allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to pepper components.

items.title: Sodium content when salted
items.content: If the pepper is prepared with added salt, consider its contribution to daily sodium limits.

items.title: Loss of heat‑sensitive vitamins with prolonged boiling
items.content: Extended cooking can reduce levels of vitamin C and other thermolabile nutrients.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Cooked red pepper can be added to salads, soups, stews, pasta, and pizza. It is also used as a puree or sandwich filling. Serve warm or chilled, optionally drizzled with olive oil, fresh herbs, or balsamic vinegar.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store cooked red pepper in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 3‑4 days. For longer keeping, freeze in portion‑sized bags – it retains flavor and texture for 2‑3 months.
